textbookText: Until the end of the nineteenth century, the history of viruses is just a part of the history of infectious diseases. The name ‘virus’ is coined by Beijerink from Latin word meaning “venom” or similar poisonous fluid. The branch of Biology that deals with the study of viruses is called virology.
Viruses are ultramicroscopic acellular obligatory parasites having either DNA or RNA as a genetic material and can replicate only inside the living host cell.

Viruses have following characteristics: 1. Viruses are ultramicroscopic intracellular parasites. 2. They are acellular i.e. they do not have cellular level of organization. 3. They are obligate parasite and can multiply only within living host cell as they lack enzyme system. 4. Viruses do not have a system to produce ATP. 5. They contain only a single type of nucleic acid, either DNA or RNA. 6. The nucleic acids are enclosed by proteinous coat called capsid.
7. Viruses are host specific i.e. they infect only a single species and definite cells of the host organisms.
8. They can be crystallized and store like chemicals i.e. Outside the cell, they behave like inert chemicals.

9. They exhibit mutation. 10. They are infectious and are capable of spreading diseases. 11. They show an incubation period, like other parasites. 12. They do not show the biological process like respiration, excretion etc. 13. They have high specific gravity. 3.2.2 STRUCTURE The shape and size of virus particles vary widely. The size of viruses ranges from 10-300 nm in diameter. The viruses may be rod-shaped, filamentous, roughly spherical, tadpole like etc. Viruses are non-living objects, because they lack cellular organization and protoplasm. However, the structure of virus consists of two main types of chemicals viz. nucleic acid (about 6%) and protein (about 96%). Nucleic acid presents at the center and form core. Nucleic acid exists either in the form of DNA or RNA or both. DNA or RNA may be single-stranded or double-stranded. Single-stranded DNA and double-stranded RNA are characteristics never found in living system and, hence unique to the viruses.

Figure 3.2.1 Structure of viruses The protein molecule surrounds around the nucleic acid filament and forms the protective sheath called as capsid. This capsid is formed of identical repeated subunits called capsomeres. Size, shape, arrangement, and composition of sub-units are specific characteristics, i.e. fixed for each type of virus. The combined structure formed by the core and capsid is termed as nucleocapsid. In some viruses, there is a thin envelope around the capsid that resembles typical cell membrane having a phospholipid bilayer. Viruses possess lysozyme in the region of their contact with host cell by the help of which they drill a hole in the host’s cell.
Viruses have both positive effects as well as negative effects:

Positive effects: 1. Viruses act as simple systems, which can be used as tools for research and analysis. Studies on recombinant DNA technology were developed using bacteriophages (Bacterial Viruses). 2. The lysogenic life cycle of certain viruses allows easy manipulation of the viral genome. Viruses are used as vectors to deliver therapeutic genes into humans in gene therapy. 3. They are also used to cure cancer in several ways like virotherapy and VDEPT (virus directed enzyme pro drug therapy). 4. Viruses are also the primary sources of vaccines used to prevent the viral infections. 5. Some of the viruses can also be used for the control of insect pests of our crop plants. 6. Some virus infected plant parts appear beautifully variegated. E.g. Tulip flowers. 7. Viruses may destroy the bacterial cells and make water free from bacteria.

Negative effects: 1. Viruses cause diseases in plants and animals including human beings. 2. Viruses cause danger to many biochemical industries especially bacteriophages that destroy the useful bacteria for such industries. 3. Viruses may be used as biological weapons.
